doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

chapter: Basie band: origins, sound and style
title: Why Basie played so few minor-key tunes
summary: Minor tunes were more common in the 1940s and early 50s; they still sounded cheerful.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You know I want to ask you something that I seem to have noticed, and just tell me am I right? After listening to many, many, many Basie albums, there’s very few tunes in minor keys. Is that right?
I don’t know. It seems like back in the early 50’s we played quite a few minor things.
Yes, in the early 50’s and going back in the 40’s, there were several more perhaps, than we did in the 60’s and 70’s and 80’s, cause “Topsy” was one of them, what’s that thing — “Tickle Toe?”
“Tickle Toe” by Prez was one of them. And there was one—
They still kind of sounded up, though.
Yeah, they sounded happy no matter what.
Yeah, well I never thought about it from that perspective but they did sound cheerful, cheerfully minor.
